title: T1567 — Exfiltration Over Web Service
subtitle: Interactive walkthrough of Exfiltration Over Web Service with the technique-specific attack path and defender evidence.

steps.title: Beachhead
steps.caption: A phishing email gave the attacker a foothold on the workstation. A user opened an attachment and the malware called home.
steps.defender: nothing yet - no alert has fired; EDR will show the phishing process only in a later hunt.

steps.title: Choosing a trusted road out
steps.caption: The attacker picks a well-known file-sharing site - not because it is special, but because company policy allows that category.
steps.defender: still no alert, and this is the design problem: the category is “allowed”, the destination is trusted, and nobody has baselined how much data should leave this subnet.

steps.title: The upload
steps.caption: The workstation pushes roughly 800 MB with steady HTTPS POST requests - POST is the web request method that sends data to a server; the user agent pretends to be a normal sync tool. Evidence: Proxy POST row
steps.defender: the proxy writes one row per request - URL, bytes out, user agent - and the per-host volume crosses its 30-day baseline.

steps.caption: Correlation shows a first-ever SaaS category from this subnet plus a rare user agent. Evidence: CASB unmanaged-app alert
steps.defender: a CASB “unmanaged app” alert fires; the analyst opens a ticket and calls the user.

steps.title: Attacker retrieves
steps.caption: On their own machine, outside your network, the attacker downloads the archive from the service using their account.
steps.defender: nothing in the corporate network - this hop happens entirely outside your telemetry. That blind spot is why early detection of the upload matters so much.

steps.title: Verdict
steps.caption: The SOC links the baseline break, the new SaaS category, and the staged archive into one incident. Egress policy for storage categories is rewritten; consumer storage is blocked by default. Evidence: Baseline-break ticket, Egress policy change
steps.defender: the lasting lesson - baselines beat single events, because the volume change was visible before any signature knew the tool.
